title: SSH from the couch
summary: Type commands on the old PC from your laptop on the house network. Don't open port 22 to the internet.

start.body:
SSH is a way to type commands on the lab computer from your normal one, over the house network.

Same idea as sitting at its keyboard — minus the closet trip.

gloss.body:
Plain words:

• SSH = Secure Shell — encrypted remote typing
• Host = the lab computer
• Host key = the lab's ID fingerprint; you accept it once
• Port 22 = the door SSH usually listens on (keep it inside the house)

You will not open that door to the public internet today.

where.body:
Where to type the command:

• Windows: Terminal or PowerShell (built-in on recent Windows)
• Mac: Terminal (Spotlight → Terminal)
• Linux: Terminal

Same command everywhere.

cmd.body:
Type:

```
ssh you@that-address
```

Examples:
ssh ender@192.168.1.50
ssh labuser@lab.local

Use the username from install and the address from hostname -I or the router list.

trust.body:
First time it says the authenticity of host can't be established — that's the host key.

Type yes and Enter. Then type the password. Nothing appears as you type; that's normal. Press Enter.

What success looks like: a prompt like you@lab:~$ ready for commands.

ok.body:
Good. Try:

hostname
uptime
exit

exit leaves SSH and returns you to your laptop.

house-only.body:
Keep SSH on the house network only.

Don't forward port 22 on the router. Don't put the lab on the public internet for "easy access." Later you can use a VPN if you need away-from-home access.

keys-later.body:
When password login has been boring for a week, put an SSH key on the laptop (a file that proves it's you — no password each time).

Skip fail2ban, changing the port, and hardening guides on day one.

refused.body:
Connection refused or timed out usually means: computer off, wrong address, or SSH software not installed.

Confirm the address. Same Wi‑Fi (not guest). Ping if you know how — optional.

refused-fix.body:
With a screen on the lab box:

```
sudo apt install openssh-server
```

Then check it's running:
sudo systemctl status ssh

If a firewall (ufw) is on:
sudo ufw allow OpenSSH
sudo ufw status

refused-retry.body:
Try ssh again from the laptop.

Still stuck? Reboot the lab once. Verify hostname -I didn't change. Temporarily connect with a cable if you're on flaky Wi‑Fi.

denied.body:
Permission denied = wrong user or password.

Use the user you created at install — not Administrator, not root (unless you set a root password on purpose), not pi unless you named it pi.

denied-tips.body:
Tips:

• Capslock off
• Try the password at the physical keyboard login first
• Username is case-sensitive
• If you locked yourself out, use the screen + keyboard on the lab to reset — don't expose SSH to the internet to "fix" it

stuck-deep.body:
If you're still stuck:

1. Sit at the lab with a screen
2. Confirm you can log in locally
3. Confirm openssh-server is installed
4. From the lab, note hostname -I again
5. From the laptop, ssh to that exact number

Pause rather than opening ports on the router.

wrap.body:
SSH from the couch is the everyday habit.

The next guided projects build on a box you can reach without walking to the closet.

end.body:
You have reached the end of this walkthrough: SSH is demystified, house-only, and troubleshooting paths are mapped.

Don't forward port 22.

address-recap.body:
Need the address again?

On the lab (with screen): hostname -I

You'll see one or more numbers. Prefer the one starting with 192.168. or 10. — those are house-network addresses.

prompt.body:
After login, the prompt often looks like:

```
username@hostname:~$
```

~ means your home folder. $ means a normal user (not root). Type commands here; they run on the lab, not on your laptop.

guest-wifi.body:
Guest Wi‑Fi and "AP isolation" often block laptop↔lab traffic.

Put both devices on the main house network. Or use ethernet for the lab.

key-preview.body:
SSH keys (later): your laptop holds a private key; the lab stores the matching public key.

Then ssh works without typing a password. Learn it after password SSH is boring and reliable.

no-portforward.body:
Router screens sometimes show "port forwarding" or "virtual server."

Do not forward 22 to the lab. That publishes SSH to the whole internet. House network only.
